concept_name: Ionic Bonding — Electron Transfer and the Endless Lattice
section: Class 11 Chemistry Ch.4 'Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure', §4.2 — Ionic or Electrovalent Bond
source_book: NCERT Chemistry Class 11, Ch.4 'Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure', §4.2 'Ionic or Electrovalent Bond' and §4.2.1 'Lattice Enthalpy' — chapter-index scope reference only; teaching, sequence, examples and phrasing authored from first principles. NCERT Exemplar consulted for misconception beliefs only (NaCl is a molecule; the whole lattice fails at once when it melts; solid salt conducts). No problem text, figure or prose imported. Desk 2, concept 1 of 2 in the Phase-0 bonding wave, on the bonding_scene scenario (field_3d, all four E3b scenario dispatches: site-layer parity, the property table and melt law, layer-shift and like_contacts, ion drift and the field cue).

real_world_anchor.primary: A grain of table salt always breaks into flat, shiny faces instead of denting or crumbling when crushed — because sliding one layer of the crystal by a single ion's width lines up ions of the same charge, and their repulsion snaps the crystal apart along that plane.
real_world_anchor.secondary: Magnesium oxide is used to line furnaces that run past 3000 kelvin, because its ions carry double the charge of salt's ions at a smaller spacing, giving it a far stronger lattice and a far higher melting point.

concept_tier_note: Tier: diamond, capabilities 3 + 4. A whiteboard draws one Na atom and one Cl atom exchanging an electron and stopping there. It cannot show the pair failing to stay a pair — a lattice that keeps growing past the frame in every direction (capability 3) — and it cannot make a crystal actually split along a plane, actually melt at a derived temperature, or actually conduct only once molten, each one a real motion driven by the same underlying charges rather than an asserted outcome (capability 4).

aha_moment.statement: There is no molecule of salt — ions keep joining into one endless lattice.
aha_moment.visual_confirmation: The lattice keeps growing past the frame instead of stopping at the one ion pair the state opens on.

separation_pm.formula: live centre-to-centre distance of the two leading sites, engine-derived from the approach ramp, converted through pm_per_unit

coordination.formula: count of nearest-neighbour sites of the opposite charge, and independently of the same charge's own sublattice, at the minimum interior-site distance

like_contacts.formula: unscreened same-charge nearest-neighbour contacts at the shifted lattice, minus the same count at the unshifted reference lattice, at the same instant

melting_point.formula: BS_ION_PAIRS[pair].mp_K for the live ion pair

lattice_enthalpy.formula: BS_ION_PAIRS[pair].lattice_kJ for the live ion pair

conductivity.formula: f_melt(T_K, pair) = clamp((T_K - pair.mp_K) / 25, 0, 1); f_melt > 0 prints the molten reading, f_melt = 0 prints 'ions fixed'

constraints: charge is conserved at every instant: Σq = 0 before, during, and after the S2 transfer ramp (charge and radius ramp in lockstep, never independently)
every ion-pair formula unit is 1:1 across all five ion pairs (NaCl, KCl, LiF, MgO, CaO) -- MgO and CaO's higher ionic charge (2+/2-) changes lattice strength, never the site-count ratio

like_contacts is a delta against the unshifted reference lattice at the same t, never a raw nearest-neighbour count -- reads 0 pre-shift and settles at a derived count post-shift; if the engine's derived count differs from the Phase-0 design expectation of 6, that is a Phase-0 arc discrepancy to report, never to tune toward
the melt outcome is derived solely from (T_K, pair.mp_K, site index, state-local t) -- no state JSON in this concept may assert that a pair has melted
coordination prints two independently-derived neighbour counts (cation-neighbours : anion-neighbours) -- never a hard-coded pair and never one count doubled to produce the other
rock-salt coordination is 6 for every interior site across all five ion pairs -- geometry sets this number, not charge magnitude

no ion-pair table digit (a_pm, mp_K, lattice_kJ) is altered from the ratified table; lattice_kJ is always the Born-Haber-derived dissociation value, never a Born-Lande/Kapustinskii calculated substitute

no authored string in this concept types a separation digit, a like_contacts digit, a coordination digit, or a solid-side conductivity digit -- those HUD lines are the only instrument, and the conductivity HUD never quotes a molten:solid ratio

STATE_1.title: One spare electron, one gap
STATE_1.label: Sodium has one spare outer electron; chlorine has one gap in its outer shell

tts_sentences.text_en: The dots are the outer electrons.
Sodium's outer shell holds one electron more than a full shell; chlorine's holds one fewer.
Count the dots as the atoms turn: one spare, one gap.
This mismatch is why sodium and chlorine react.

STATE_2.title: The electron transfers
STATE_2.label: The electron transfers from sodium to chlorine, and both atoms change size

tts_sentences.text_en: Chlorine pulls electrons far harder than sodium holds them, so the spare electron moves across — watch it.
Sodium loses its whole outer shell and gets smaller; chlorine gains one electron and gets larger.
Two charged ions now, and the readout shows both new sizes.

STATE_3.title: The ions pull in and stop
STATE_3.label: Attraction pulls the two ions together; their full inner shells stop them at a fixed spacing

scene_composition.text: Full shells cannot overlap — they stop here

tts_sentences.text_en: Opposite charges pull the ions together.
The closer they get, the harder their full inner shells push back.
Pull in, push out, balance: the ions settle at a fixed spacing.
The distance readout shows the spacing live.

STATE_4.title: Not a molecule — a lattice
STATE_4.label: The pair does not stay a pair — ions keep joining until the lattice runs past the frame

scene_composition.text: The pattern repeats in every direction
This block is a tiny corner of one grain

tts_sentences.text_en: Here is the pair most people picture as 'a molecule of salt.'
But a chloride ion pulls every sodium ion near it, not just one — watch.
Ions keep joining, in a strict alternating pattern, and nothing stops the growth.
Salt is not molecules. It is one endless repeating lattice.

misconception_watch.belief: NaCl is a molecule — one Na stuck to one Cl.
misconception_watch.visual_counter: the pair does not stay a pair; ions keep joining until the lattice runs past the frame
misconception_watch.one_line_fix: NaCl is a 1:1 ratio of ions in an endless lattice, not a molecule.

STATE_5.title: Six neighbours for every ion
STATE_5.label: Every ion in the lattice is surrounded by six of the other kind

tts_sentences.text_en: Fade the other ions and look inside the solid.
Six rods, six neighbours of the opposite charge — above, below, left, right, front, back.
Pick any ion in the whole crystal and the count is the same: six and six.

STATE_6.title: One layer shift splits it
STATE_6.label: A one-site layer shift lines up ions of the same charge, and the crystal splits

scene_composition.text: A one-site slide lines up like charges
If like charges line up, they push the halves apart

tts_sentences.text_en: This is why a salt grain splits into flat faces instead of denting.
Slide the top half of the crystal by one position.
Every plus now sits over a plus, every minus over a minus.
The counter shows the new like-charge contacts — and the crystal splits along that plane.

STATE_7.title: Why the melting point is high
STATE_7.label: Heat frees the ions at the melting point — no single bond breaks alone

scene_composition.text: Ions become free at the melting point

tts_sentences.text_en: Heat the crystal and every ion shakes harder, but each is held by six neighbours, and those by six more — no single weak bond breaks first.
An ion is freed only once that whole surrounding pull is overcome.
That is why the melting point is so high — the readout shows the temperature and energy needed.

STATE_8.title: Only molten salt conducts
STATE_8.label: The same field acts on a solid and a molten sample — only the free ions carry charge

scene_composition.text: The same field acts on both
Free ions can move and carry current

tts_sentences.text_en: Both samples are pure salt, and the same push acts on both.
In the solid, every ion is held at its site — it is pulled slightly, and stays in place.
In the molten sample the ions are free, and they drift: plus one way, minus the other.
Moving charge is a current.

misconception_watch.belief: Solid salt conducts — it is full of charges.
misconception_watch.visual_counter: the same field on both samples: the solid's ions are held at their sites and do not move; only the melt's free ions drift
misconception_watch.one_line_fix: Charge must be free to move to carry current — molten or dissolved, not solid.

STATE_9.title: Higher charge, stronger lattice
STATE_9.label: One shared heater, two crystals — salt melts on the way up while magnesium oxide holds

scene_composition.text: Furnace walls are lined with magnesium oxide

tts_sentences.text_en: Same heater, two crystals.
Salt's ions carry single charges; magnesium oxide's carry double charges and sit closer together.
Both its melting point and its lattice-dissociation energy are far higher — different measurements of the same stronger attraction, not the same quantity.
Salt melts as the temperature rises; magnesium oxide stays solid.

STATE_10.label: Pick an ion pair, and drag temperature, layer shift or field to see the lattice respond

regeneration_variants.label: Same electron-transfer-and-lattice reasoning, potassium and fluorine instead of sodium and chlorine
regeneration_variants.physical_world: Potassium's single outer electron transfers to fluorine's single vacancy, forming K+ and F- ions that pack into the same 1:1 alternating rock-salt lattice, cleave along the same planes, and conduct only once molten.
regeneration_variants.same_physics: Identical one-electron-transfer mechanism, identical 1:1 ionic ratio, identical 6:6 coordination geometry, and identical brittle-cleavage, high-melting-point and molten-only-conduction properties; only the specific pair of elements and their exact radius, melting point and lattice enthalpy change.
